title: How to work a French knot in cross-stitch
subtitle: The raised dot used for eyes, flower centres, and texture
excerpt: A French knot is a small raised dot formed by wrapping the thread around the needle two or three times before pushing it back through the same fabric hole. It is the stitch for animal eyes, flower centres, berry clusters, and any detail that needs to sit slightly off the fabric surface.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, embroidery chapter. French knot technique is documented consistently across all major Victorian needlework references including Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small raised dot worked by wrapping the thread around the needle two or three times, then pushing the needle back through the same fabric hole and pulling the thread through the wraps. The wraps sit on the surface as a tight raised node.

content.text: A
French knot

is a small raised dot. You bring the thread up through the fabric, wrap it around the needle, then push the needle back down through the same hole while holding the wrap in place with a finger. The thread tightens around the needle shaft as it passes through, forming a tight node on the surface.
French knots appear after the
cross-stitch fill
and after the
back-stitch outline
are both complete. Working them last avoids the needle catching the outline thread while forming the knots.
Working the knot
Come up at the knot position.
Bring the needle up through the fabric at the hole where you want the knot to sit. Pull the thread through until only a short tail remains on the back.
Hold the thread and wrap the needle.

Hold the thread taut with the off-hand about three centimetres from the fabric. Pass the needle under the thread from right to left, then wrap the thread around the needle shaft twice (for a standard-size knot) or three times (for a larger knot). Keep the wraps close together near the fabric.
Hold the wrap and push the needle down.

Keep the off-hand finger pressing the wraps against the needle shaft and fabric. Push the needle back down through the same hole, or one thread away from it. Do not move the needle far: the wraps need to be right at the fabric surface.
Pull through slowly.

Keep the off-hand pressing the wraps flat against the fabric until the needle is almost fully through. Let the thread slip through the wraps gradually: pulling too fast yanks the knot through the hole. A correctly pulled knot stays on the surface as a tight raised dot.
Common problems

items.symptom: The knot disappears through the fabric hole
items.cause: The needle went down through the exact same hole it came up from, or the thread was pulled too fast.
items.fix: Move the needle one fabric thread away from the entry hole before pushing down. Pull slowly, keeping the wraps pressed against the fabric surface until the very last moment.

items.symptom: The knot is very small or flat
items.cause: The wraps were too loose, or only one wrap was used.
items.fix: Keep the off-hand thread taut while wrapping. Two tight wraps give a standard knot; three give a larger one. The wraps should feel firm against the needle shaft.

items.symptom: The knot is uneven or lumpy
items.cause: The wraps were placed far from the fabric or spaced apart on the needle.
items.fix: Wrap close to the fabric and keep the wraps tightly together on the needle shaft. The shorter the distance from fabric to wrap, the neater the knot.

content.text: What comes next

The woven wheel and the lazy daisy extend the textured decoration vocabulary beyond the French knot. Both are worked on the surface of the fabric and appear as embellishments on floral cross-stitch charts.
